All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?
</problem>

7	We prove both directions. The lower-bound construction below is elementary; in particular, it does not require the Kneser graph theorem. The upper bound uses the standard degree form of Szemerédi’s regularity lemma.
8	
9	## 1. Preliminary observations
10	
11	For a graph \(G\), define its **odd cube** \(F(G)\) on \(V(G)\): two distinct vertices are adjacent if there is a walk of length \(1\) or \(3\) between them in \(G\).
12	
13	A graph with no \(C_3\) or \(C_5\) has no closed odd walk of length \(3\) or \(5\). Indeed, every closed odd walk contains an odd cycle of at most its length.
14	
15	Consequently, if \(G\) has no \(C_3,C_5\), then:
16	
17	* endpoints of a length-\(3\) walk are distinct;
18	* if \(xy\in E(F(G))\), then
19	  \[
20	  N_G(x)\cap N_G(y)=\varnothing. \tag{1}
21	  \]
22	  A common neighbor would complete a closed odd walk of length \(3\) or \(5\).
23	
24	We will use the following conversion.
25	
26	### Lemma 1: a bounded coloring of the odd cube gives the required target
27	
28	For every positive integer \(q\), there is a finite triangle-free graph \(U_q\) such that
29	\[
30	\chi(F(G))\le q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad G\longrightarrow U_q.
31	\]
32	
33	**Proof.**
34	The vertices of \(U_q\) are pairs
35	\[
36	(a,A),\qquad a\in[q],\quad A\subseteq[q]\setminus\{a\}.
37	\]
38	Put an edge between \((a,A)\) and \((b,B)\) precisely when
39	\[
40	b\in A,\qquad a\in B,\qquad A\cap B=\varnothing. \tag{2}
41	\]
42	This graph is triangle-free: in a triangle with first coordinates \(a,b,d\), the first coordinate \(a\) would belong to both sets attached to the other two vertices, contradicting their adjacency.
43	
44	Let \(\phi\) be a proper \(q\)-coloring of \(F(G)\), and set
45	\[
46	A_v=\{\phi(w):w\in N_G(v)\}.
47	\]
48	Map \(v\) to \((\phi(v),A_v)\). For \(uv\in E(G)\), the reciprocal membership conditions in (2) hold. Moreover, \(A_u\cap A_v=\varnothing\): otherwise equally colored vertices would be joined by a length-\(3\) walk through \(u,v\). Thus the map is a homomorphism. ∎
49	
50	---
51	
52	## 2. Upper bound: every \(c>1/9\) works
53	
54	We prove that, for fixed \(c>1/9\), the odd cubes of the graphs in question have bounded chromatic number.
55	
56	### Regularity tool
57	
58	We use this standard degree-form regularity lemma.
59	
60	For every \(\varepsilon,d>0\), there is \(M\) such that every sufficiently large graph \(G\) has a spanning subgraph \(G'\) and a partition
61	\[
62	V(G)=V_0\sqcup V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k
63	\]
64	satisfying:
65	
66	1. \(k\le M\), \(|V_0|\le\varepsilon n\), and
67	   \[
68	   |V_1|=\cdots=|V_k|=m;
69	   \]
70	2. every vertex loses at most \((d+\varepsilon)n\) incident edges:
71	   \[
72	   d_{G'}(v)\ge d_G(v)-(d+\varepsilon)n;
73	   \]
74	3. every \(V_i\), \(i\ge1\), is independent in \(G'\);
75	4. each pair \(V_i,V_j\), \(i,j\ge1\), is either empty in \(G'\), or is \(\varepsilon\)-regular with density at least \(d\).
76	
77	Edges incident with \(V_0\) need not be deleted. This is the usual degree form of the regularity lemma. Small graphs can be included by enlarging \(M\) and using singleton clusters.
78	
79	Fix
80	\[
81	0<\varepsilon<\min\left\{\frac{c-1/9}{8},\frac1{10}\right\},
82	\qquad d=4\varepsilon,
83	\qquad \beta=c-8\varepsilon>\frac19. \tag{3}
84	\]
85	
86	Apply the lemma to a graph \(G\) with no \(C_3,C_5\) and minimum degree at least \(cn\).
87	
88	Let \(R\) be the reduced graph on \([k]\), with \(ij\in E(R)\) when the corresponding pair is nonempty. For \(S\subseteq[k]\), write
89	\[
90	w(S)=m|S|,\qquad N_R(S)=\bigcup_{i\in S}N_R(i).
91	\]
92	
93	For every \(i\),
94	\[
95	w(N_R(i))\ge(c-6\varepsilon)n\ge\beta n. \tag{4}
96	\]
97	Indeed, a vertex in \(V_i\) has at least \((c-5\varepsilon)n\) neighbors in \(G'\), and at most \(\varepsilon n\) of these are in \(V_0\). In particular, \(R\) has no isolated vertices.
98	
99	### Supports
100	
101	Define the support of any vertex \(v\in V(G)\), including vertices of \(V_0\), by
102	\[
103	\sigma(v)=
104	\left\{i:\ |N_{G'}(v)\cap V_i|\ge2\varepsilon m\right\}.
105	\]
106	
107	At least \(\beta n\) neighbors of \(v\) lie in its support clusters:
108	\[
109	\left|N_{G'}(v)\cap\bigcup_{i\in\sigma(v)}V_i\right|
110	\ge(c-5\varepsilon-\varepsilon-2\varepsilon)n
111	=\beta n. \tag{5}
112	\]
113	Thus every support is nonempty.
114	
115	Here are the regularity consequences we need.
116	
117	### Support rules
118	
119	For vertices \(x,y\):
120	
121	1. \(\sigma(x)\) is independent in \(R\).
122	2. If \(xy\in E(G)\), then
123	   \[
124	   \sigma(x)\cap\sigma(y)=\varnothing,
125	   \qquad
126	   N_R(\sigma(x))\cap N_R(\sigma(y))=\varnothing. \tag{6}
127	   \]
128	3. If \(xzy\) is a length-\(2\) walk in \(G\), there is no \(R\)-edge between \(\sigma(x)\) and \(\sigma(y)\).
129	
130	We justify all three. Across an \(R\)-edge, any two prescribed subsets of the two clusters, each of size at least \(2\varepsilon m\), have an edge between them. Across an \(R\)-walk \(i-j-\ell\), any such prescribed subsets of \(V_i,V_\ell\) are joined by a length-\(2\) walk through \(V_j\). For the latter assertion, each prescribed subset has neighbors in more than \((1-\varepsilon)m\) vertices of \(V_j\), so their neighbor sets intersect.
131	
132	An \(R\)-edge inside \(\sigma(x)\) therefore gives a closed \(3\)-walk through \(x\), proving rule 1.
133	
134	A common vertex of \(N_R(\sigma(x))\) and \(N_R(\sigma(y))\) gives a length-\(4\) walk from \(x\) to \(y\). Together with \(xy\), this is a forbidden closed \(5\)-walk. This proves the second assertion of (6). If the supports shared an index \(i\), a neighbor of \(i\) in \(R\) would be such a common vertex; hence their supports are disjoint as well.
135	
136	Finally, an \(R\)-edge between the supports of the endpoints of \(xzy\) gives a length-\(3\) walk between those endpoints. Together with \(xzy\), this is a forbidden closed \(5\)-walk. This proves rule 3.
137	
138	Using closed walks, rather than insisting that all chosen vertices are distinct, eliminates any coincidence issues.
139	
140	### Low supports are independent in the odd cube
141	
142	Call a support \(S\) **low** if
143	\[
144	w(S)<2\beta n.
145	\]
146	The vertices having any one low support form an independent set in \(F(G)\). Otherwise (1) and (5) would give two disjoint sets of neighbors, each of size at least \(\beta n\), both contained in a set of size less than \(2\beta n\).
147	
148	Now color every vertex \(v\) by the pair
149	\[
150	\mathcal C(v)=
151	\left(
152	\sigma(v),\
153	\{\sigma(u):u\in N_G(v)\}
154	\right). \tag{7}
155	\]
156	There are at most
157	\[
158	Q=2^M\,2^{2^M} \tag{8}
159	\]
160	possible colors, independently of \(n\).
161	
162	We claim that (7) properly colors \(F(G)\).
163	
164	Suppose otherwise. Two same-colored vertices cannot be adjacent in \(G\), by (6). Thus there is a length-\(3\) walk
165	\[
166	x-a-b-y,\qquad \mathcal C(x)=\mathcal C(y).
167	\]
168	Put
169	\[
170	S=\sigma(x)=\sigma(y),\qquad T=\sigma(a),\qquad U=\sigma(b).
171	\]
172	
173	All three supports are non-low:
174	
175	* \(S\) is non-low because \(x,y\) are adjacent in \(F(G)\).
176	* If \(T\) were low, then, because \(x,y\) have the same color, \(y\) would have a neighbor \(a'\) with support \(T\). But \(a-b-y-a'\) is a length-\(3\) walk, contradicting the odd-cube independence of support class \(T\).
177	* The same argument shows that \(U\) is non-low.
178	
179	Therefore
180	\[
181	w(S),w(T),w(U)\ge2\beta n. \tag{9}
182	\]
183	
184	The actual edges \(xa,ab,by\), together with (6), show that \(S,T,U\) are pairwise disjoint and that
185	\[
186	N_R(S),N_R(T),N_R(U)
187	\]
188	are pairwise disjoint.
189	
190	Moreover, \(S\cup T\cup U\) is independent in \(R\). Internal edges are excluded by rule 1. Cross-edges between \(S,U\) and between \(T,S\) are excluded by the walks \(x-a-b\) and \(a-b-y\). Finally, because \(x,y\) have the same color and \(y\) has a neighbor of support \(U\), so does \(x\); say that neighbor is \(b'\). The walk \(a-x-b'\) excludes cross-edges between \(T,U\).
191	
192	It follows that these six sets are pairwise disjoint:
193	\[
194	S,\ T,\ U,\ N_R(S),\ N_R(T),\ N_R(U).
195	\]
196	Every support is nonempty, so (4) gives each of the last three sets weight at least \(\beta n\). Together with (9),
197	\[
198	n\ge 3(2\beta n)+3(\beta n)=9\beta n>n,
199	\]
200	a contradiction.
201	
202	Thus \(\chi(F(G))\le Q\). Lemma 1 supplies the fixed finite triangle-free target \(U_Q\). This proves that every \(c>1/9\) has the required property.
203	
204	---
205	
206	## 3. Lower bound: no \(c<1/9\) works
207	
208	We first construct graphs with arbitrarily large chromatic number whose vertices have equal-sized labels, with adjacent labels disjoint and occupying nearly half the label universe.
209	
210	### Elementary shift graphs
211	
212	For integers \(N\ge k\), let \(S(N,k)\) have the increasing \(k\)-tuples from \([N]\) as vertices. For every increasing \((k+1)\)-tuple, join its first and last \(k\)-windows:
213	\[
214	(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\sim(x_2,\ldots,x_{k+1}).
215	\]
216	
217	For each fixed \(k\), these graphs have unbounded chromatic number as \(N\to\infty\).
218	
219	To see this, a proper \(h\)-coloring of \(S(N,j)\) induces a coloring of \(S(N,j-1)\) with at most \(2^h\) colors: color a tuple by the set of colors of all its right-extensions. Consecutive \((j-1)\)-windows get different sets, since the color of their combined \(j\)-tuple belongs to the first set and cannot belong to the second.
220	
221	Iterating down to \(S(N,1)=K_N\) proves the assertion.
222	
223	Now fix an odd \(k\ge3\), and put \(F=S(N,k)\). Index \(m=N!\) coordinates by permutations \(\pi\) of \([N]\). Give a vertex \(v=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\) the label
224	\[
225	L(v)=
226	\{\pi:\text{the \(\pi\)-least element of \(v\) occurs at an even position}\}.
227	\]
228	Every label has the same size
229	\[
230	r=\frac{k-1}{2k}\,m. \tag{10}
231	\]
232	Moreover,
233	\[
234	uv\in E(F)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L(u)\cap L(v)=\varnothing. \tag{11}
235	\]
236	
237	For (11), consider the combined \((k+1)\)-tuple of two adjacent windows. If its least element is internal, its positions in the two windows have opposite parity. If it is an endpoint, one window has its minimum at position \(1\) or \(k\), both odd.
238	
239	### Densifying a three-edge subdivision
240	
241	Fix \(c<1/9\) and a finite triangle-free graph \(H\). Write \(h=\max\{1,|V(H)|\}\).
242	
243	Choose an odd \(k\) sufficiently large that
244	\[
245	c<\frac{r}{3(m+r)}
246	=\frac{k-1}{3(3k-1)}. \tag{12}
247	\]
248	Choose \(N\) large enough that \(\chi(F)>h\), where \(F=S(N,k)\).
249	
250	Orient the edges of \(F\) arbitrarily and replace each oriented edge \(u\to v\) by
251	\[
252	u-a_{uv}-b_{uv}-v.
253	\]
254	Call this subdivision \(D\). Assign types \(0,1,2\) respectively to original vertices, \(a\)-vertices, and \(b\)-vertices. Assign labels along each subdivided edge as follows:
255	\[
256	\begin{array}{c|cccc}
257	\text{vertex}&u&a_{uv}&b_{uv}&v\\ \hline
258	\text{label}&L(u)&L(v)&L(u)&L(v).
259	\end{array} \tag{13}
260	\]
261	
262	A useful property is:
263	\[
264	\begin{split}
265	&\text{every length-\(3\) walk in \(D\) whose endpoints have the same type}\\
266	&\text{has endpoints with disjoint labels.} \tag{14}
267	\end{split}
268	\]
269	Indeed, its type sequence must go cyclically through \(0,1,2,0\), in one direction or the other. At least one internal vertex is a subdivision vertex of degree \(2\); its two neighbors have equal labels by (13). The two endpoint labels are therefore labels of endpoints of an edge of \(F\), so (11) applies.
270	
271	For each type \(i\in\{0,1,2\}\), add:
272	
273	* a set \(W_i\) consisting of \(q\) copies of each of the \(m\) coordinates;
274	* a set \(P_i\) of \(rq\) vertices;
275	* all edges between \(W_i\) and \(P_i\);
276	* for every type-\(i\) vertex \(x\) of \(D\), edges from \(x\) to the copies of the coordinates in its label.
277	
278	Let the resulting graph be \(G\), and write \(s=|V(D)|\). Then
279	\[
280	|V(G)|=s+3(m+r)q,\qquad \delta(G)\ge rq. \tag{15}
281	\]
282	By (12), choosing \(q\) sufficiently large makes
283	\[
284	rq\ge c\bigl[s+3(m+r)q\bigr].
285	\]
286	
287	### There are no \(C_3\) or \(C_5\)
288	
289	The graph \(D\) has girth at least \(9\).
290	
291	After deleting the edges of \(D\), the remaining graph is a disjoint union of three bipartite graphs, one per type. All \(D\)-vertices of a given type lie on the same side. Thus every excursion through new vertices has positive even length and joins same-type \(D\)-vertices.
292	
293	Suppose an odd cycle of length at most \(5\) is not entirely in \(D\). It must use an odd number of \(D\)-edges:
294	
295	* One \(D\)-edge is impossible: it changes type, whereas all excursions preserve type.
296	* Three \(D\)-edges force exactly one two-edge excursion. Thus a length-\(3\) path in \(D\) has same-type endpoints sharing a coordinate, contrary to (14).
297	
298	So \(G\) contains neither \(C_3\) nor \(C_5\).
299	
300	### There is no homomorphism to \(H\)
301	
302	Under a homomorphism \(G\to H\), the endpoints of every subdivided edge of \(F\) must have different images. Otherwise its three-edge path would map to a closed \(3\)-walk in the simple triangle-free graph \(H\).
303	
304	The restriction to the original vertices would therefore properly color \(F\) with at most \(|V(H)|\) colors, contradicting \(\chi(F)>h\).
305	
306	We have constructed the required counterexample for every finite triangle-free \(H\). Thus no \(c<1/9\) has the property.
307	
308	Combining the two halves proves the claimed infimum. Whether the property holds exactly at \(c=1/9\) is unnecessary for this conclusion.
309	
310	---
311	
312	## 4. Executable finite verification
313	
314	The proof above handles all sizes. The following self-contained Python additionally checks the finite constructions and combinatorial mechanisms—not merely the asserted answer.
315	
316	It verifies:
317	
318	* the universal targets \(U_q\) for \(q\le5\);
319	* the odd-cube-to-target map on all \(150\) nonempty \(C_3,C_5\)-free graph-atlas graphs through seven vertices;
320	* all six-set configurations on reduced graphs through five vertices;
321	* permutation labels, extension-color reduction, minimum degrees, and absence of \(C_3,C_5\) in two complete lower-bound constructions.
322	
323	For cycle exclusion it computes exact integer traces: in a simple graph, \(\operatorname{tr}(A^3)=\operatorname{tr}(A^5)=0\) is equivalent to having no \(C_3,C_5\).
